urgent.heading: Urgent — call now
urgent.primary_message: Use the blue reliever inhaler with spacer. If no improvement in 10 minutes — call 10177.
red_flags: Too breathless to speak in full sentences, or to cry
Lips, fingernails, or face turning blue or grey
Skin sucking in between or below the ribs with each breath
Reliever inhaler not helping at all
Drowsy, confused, or exhausted from breathing effort
Cough so severe the child cannot stop or sleep
Silent chest — the wheeze stops because airflow is too low

what_is_it.heading: Childhood asthma in plain terms
what_is_it.lede: Asthma is when the airways in the lungs become sensitive and inflamed — they tighten and produce mucus in response to triggers, making it hard for a child to breathe.
paragraphs: Childhood asthma is one of the most common chronic conditions in South African kids — about 1 in 10 children. Symptoms can come and go. With proper treatment, most children with asthma can live, play sport, and sleep normally.

Children with asthma usually need two kinds of medicine: a reliever inhaler (usually blue) for during an attack, and a preventer inhaler (usually brown) used every day to keep airways calm. The preventer is what keeps a child out of hospital — even when they feel fine.

items.headline: 1 in 10
items.body: South African children have asthma — many undiagnosed, especially those with persistent night-time cough.

items.headline: Two inhalers
items.body: Blue reliever for attacks, brown preventer every day. The preventer is what actually controls the disease.

items.headline: Always spacer
items.body: Children must always use a spacer with their inhaler. Doubles the amount of medicine that reaches the lungs.

items.headline: Triggers vary
items.body: Common triggers: viral colds, dust, smoke, pet dander, cold air, exercise. Knowing your child's triggers helps prevent attacks.

pull_quote.text: Most childhood asthma attacks bad enough for hospital could have been prevented with daily preventer inhaler use. Don't stop it because the child feels fine — that is what it is meant to do.

signs.heading: Common signs of childhood asthma
signs.lede: Asthma doesn't always look like wheezing. In children especially, a long-running dry cough — particularly at night or with exercise — is often the only sign for months before diagnosis.

items.title: Cough that won't go away
items.description: Especially at night, early morning, or with running and playing. The most common symptom in children — often missed for months as 'just a cold that keeps coming back'.

items.title: Wheezing or noisy breathing
items.description: Whistling sound, especially when breathing out. Sometimes only during colds, sometimes with any exertion.

items.title: Shortness of breath, tight chest
items.description: Child sits out at PE, can't keep up with peers, complains chest feels tight or 'sore'. Worth investigating.

myths.heading: What is true and what is not

items.myth: Children always grow out of asthma.
items.fact: Many do — but many don't. Even when symptoms settle, airway sensitivity can return at any age. Keep the preventer going as prescribed, even when fine.

The dose in inhaled preventers is very low and acts locally in the lungs. Any small effect on growth is much less harmful than poorly controlled asthma. Oral steroids during attacks have more effect — which is why prevention matters.
Well-controlled asthma should not limit sport. Many Olympic athletes have asthma. If your child can't keep up with peers, the asthma isn't controlled — talk to the clinic.

items.myth: We only need the inhaler when they're sick.
items.fact: The blue reliever is for sick days. The brown preventer must be used every day — even when fine. Skipping it lets inflammation build, leading to attacks.

items.title: Get an asthma action plan from the clinic
items.description: A written plan tells you exactly what to do at each stage — green (fine), yellow (worsening), red (emergency). Free, signed by your doctor or nurse.

items.title: Always use a spacer with the inhaler
items.description: Spacers double the amount of medicine reaching the lungs. Free at clinics. Don't let a child use an inhaler without one.

items.title: Give preventer every day, every season
items.description: Brown preventer (or combination inhaler) twice a day, every day. Even when the child feels fine. Even in summer. Skipping is the most common cause of attacks.

items.title: Know your child's triggers
items.description: Keep notes on what brings on symptoms. Common ones: cold viruses, dust, smoke (including braai), cats, dogs, cold air, exercise. Reduce what you can.

items.title: Tell the school and after-care
items.description: Give them a copy of the action plan and a spare reliever inhaler with spacer. Most schools accept these once paperwork is signed.

get_help.heading: Where to go
get_help.lede: Childhood asthma is fully treatable in the South African public system. Inhalers, spacers, and action plans are all free at clinics.
